title: Multi-lane admission with model-slimming and request budgets
creator: Sofia Alvarez
description:
Problem statement: Intermittent multi-region spikes and hardware eviction events are causing tail-latency SLO breaches for high-priority tenants. Current binary shedding (accept/reject) and coarse priority lanes (latency-first vs cost-first) lack fine-grained controls to preserve perceived quality for premium customers while throttling background or cheaper fidelity workloads.

Goal: Design and implement a multi-lane admission controller that enforces per-tenant request budgets and supports runtime 'model-slimming' graceful-degradation paths (e.g., shorter decode length, lower precision model variant, compressed response schema). The controller should integrate with existing routing/fallback logic, expose rollout flags, and emit telemetry for SLO observability and offline chargeback.

Success criteria / acceptance criteria:
- Controller enforces per-tenant and per-route budgets with 95th percentile enforcement latency <= 3ms extra processing overhead.
- Traffic that exceeds budgets is diverted to predefined degradation paths rather than immediate errors for P0/P1 tenants.
- Observable metrics exist for budget burn-rate, diverted-request fraction, and degradation quality regressions.
- Integration tests simulate region failover + spike and show SLO preservation for premium tenancy compared to current baseline.

Design proposal (high-level):
1) Multi-lane admission: classify incoming requests into dynamic lanes: "premium", "standard", "best-effort". Lanes have separate soft budgets (tokens per second) and hard caps. Lanes are programmable by policy (SLO-driven, cost-driven, or admin override).
2) Request budget engine: token-bucket per-tenant-per-route with burst allowance; supports cumulative budgets across regions (global view) and local emergency quotas when global coordination is slow.
3) Degradation catalogue (model-slimming): define a small set of canonical degradation actions per model-family: shorten max tokens, switch to quantized variant, reduce sampling temperature/beam width, or produce structured/sparse responses (drop optional fields). Each action has a cost/quality estimate in the catalogue.
4) Policy decision: when a lane exhausts budget, admission controller consults policy graph: first attempt lightweight degradations (shorten max tokens), then model swap to quantized variant, then drop non-critical output fields, finally reject. Policy is configurable per-tenant and per-route.
5) Routing & failover integration: admission controller emits enriched routing headers indicating applied degradation so downstream runtime and billing can honor fallbacks and post-hoc analysis. On region failover, emergency reweighting increases hard caps for premium lanes within safety windows.

Telemetry and observability:
- New metrics: tenant_budget_remaining, tenant_budget_burn_rate, degraded_request_count_by_action, avg_quality_delta_by_tenant, degraded_latency_tail.
- Traces: decision-path tags showing sequence of degradations applied.
- Alerts: sustained >5% degraded-request fraction for premium tenants; sudden shift in quality metrics post-deployment.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (lab): implement budget engine and catalogue in staging; unit tests for token logic and degradation application.
- Phase 1 (canary): enable for internal tenants only with non-intrusive logging of suggested degradations.
- Phase 2 (soft launch): allow automatic application of degradations for best-effort lane only. Collect quality telemetry for 2 weeks.
- Phase 3 (gradual): enable adaptive policies for standard lane and opt-in premium beta customers.

Testing plan:
- Load tests across three simulated regions with coordinated spikes and delayed global state updates. Verify budget synchronization and local emergency quotas.
- A/B tests comparing baseline admission vs multi-lane controller on latency and quality metrics.
- Synthetic quality regression harness using canonical prompt set per model family to measure effect of each degradation action.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Over-aggressive degradations may cause subtle UX regressions; mitigation: conservative default policy and opt-in aggressive modes.
- Global budget synchronization latency could cause uneven enforcement; mitigation: local emergency quotas + conservative global reconciliation.
- Billing attribution complexity when multiple degradations apply; mitigation: attach degradation headers and record action metadata for billing pipeline.

Dependencies:
- routing-service: header propagation and lane-aware route table (ENG-117203 related).
- console: UI to set per-tenant budgets and view burn rates (PM work).
- model-catalog: need metadata about quantized variants and quality cost estimates.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we expose per-tenant default degradation policies in the Console or keep them API-only for first release?
- How do we compress/represent quality deltas in telemetry (single scalar vs distribution)?
- Policy language: simple ordered list of actions vs expressive policy graph with predicates.

Next steps (short term):
- Implement prototype budget engine and a stub degradation catalogue in the runtime (E2).
- Create backlog items for console controls and billing integration.
- Schedule sync with PM (Marcus Nguyen) and design (Aisha Patel) to finalize UX for opt-in flows.

2026-03-08 Aisha Patel (Design): Suggested UI wireframes for per-tenant budget sliders and a timeline view for burn rate. Asked for examples of degradation messaging for customers.
